title: POC scoping: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private - Spectra Payments
summary: Discovery + POC scoping to decide between Hosted, Dedicated, or Private deployment. Customer wants clear success criteria (latency p95/p99 targets, cost per inference), workload sizing (qps, token profile), benchmark plan, and timeline for pilot. Security team requested SOC2 details, VPC/KMS options and data residency. Next steps: send security docs, share benchmark plan and pricing, schedule lab benchmark in 1 week.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-11 | 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Tom (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood CSM), Rachel (Spectra Head of ML), Evan (Spectra Platform), Linda (Spectra Security), Samir (Product)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving out time. Quick intro, I'm Maya Patel on the AE team, Tom Rivers is our solutions engineer and Carlos will support the POC. Could we do a quick round of intros on the Spectra side?
[00:12] Rachel: Hi, Rachel Kim, head of ML. We're looking to add LLM-based features to payments fraud detection and customer support triage.
[00:20] Evan: Evan Torres, platform engineering, I'll own infra and deployment decisions.
[00:25] Linda: Linda Park, security and compliance. I'll be the point for SOC2, encryption, and legal questions.
[00:31] Samir: Samir, product, focused on acceptance criteria and timelines.

[00:38] Maya: Great. Agenda — clarify success criteria, go through your workload, discuss Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs, and align on benchmarks and timeline.
[00:46] Rachel: Sounds good. Short context: we currently run transformer-based models in-house for embeddings and a set of heuristics. The new feature will call an LLM for triage to label suspicious transactions and generate agent summaries. Peak is around 120 qps but typical steady-state 15-20 qps, average request 350 tokens input, 150 tokens output. P95 latency target for user-facing flows is 300-400ms, but for the async fraud scoring path we can tolerate up to 1s. Cost is a big constraint — want to keep per-inference cost below $0.01 ideally.

[01:30] Tom: Thanks Rachel, that helps. Quick clarifying q's — is 120 qps a sustained burst or very rare? And what's concurrency distribution?
[01:38] Rachel: It's bursty — events happen at 3am for certain regions, and we do batch re-score nightly. Concurrency rarely exceeds 200 concurrent requests for short periods.

[01:48] Tom: Understood. For those numbers we usually map to Hosted if you want fastest time to value and lower ops. Dedicated if you need predictable throughput and lower long-term unit cost. Private if you have strict data residency or air-gap requirements.

[02:05] Evan: Can you give more detail on the predictability claim? Our infra team worries about spikes and cold starts. We need <1% failure on spikes.
[02:15] Tom: Sure — Hosted uses shared pools but we have routing priorities and auto-burst. For predictable SLA-backed throughput you'd get Dedicated where a GPU pool is reserved to your tenant, so cold starts are essentially eliminated and tail latencies are tighter. For Private you manage the infra so you control exactly how it's provisioned.

[02:40] Linda: On security — what are your encryption-in-transit and at-rest guarantees? Do you support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) and VPC peering?
[02:48] Maya: Yes, we support TLS in transit and AES-256 at rest. For Private we can integrate with your KMS/HSM and deploy in your VPC. Dedicated offers VPC peering and customer-managed KMS for certain plans — we'll confirm the exact SKU in the SOW. We'll also share our SOC2 and ISO artifacts.

[03:12] Samir: For decisions, what would you recommend we choose for the pilot? We want quick validation but also don't want to under-index on security or cost.
[03:20] Tom: Typical pattern — start with Hosted for a short pilot to validate accuracy and prompt design because it's fastest to set up, then move to Dedicated if you need predictable p99 and lower unit cost at scale, or Private if you require full network isolation and strict KMS. For Spectra's mix — given you have compliance needs but are open to demos — we often do a two-step: hosted pilot for model/quality validation, and a parallel Dedicated estimate so you know migration costs.

[03:50] Rachel: That makes sense. Our success criteria: 1) accuracy on fraud triage (measured by F1 increase vs baseline) — target 10% relative lift, 2) latency p95 < 400ms for interactive flows, p99 < 1s for scoring, 3) cost per inference under $0.01 or a clear path to that with batching/quantization, and 4) pass security checklist.

[04:18] Tom: We'll formalize a test harness. For accuracy we recommend a blind evaluation on your labeled dataset plus an adversarial prompt set. For latency we'll run a lab benchmark at your traffic profile and measure p50/p90/p95/p99. For cost we can estimate token rates and show approximate cost/1M requests for Hosted vs Dedicated. We can also show quantized model variants for Dedicated/Private which reduce GPU cost.

[04:50] Evan: Benchmarking — we need to run realistic tests. Can you run benchmarks using our sample prompts and tokens, and capture GPU type?
[04:58] Tom: Yes. We'll need a sample dataset (3-5k representative requests) and a traffic profile (qps, bursts, concurrency). We'll spin up an isolated lab benchmark — for Hosted we'll use our shared infra but controlled traffic; Dedicated we'll simulate reserved pool. We'll document hardware (GPU type), sequence length distribution, and kernel configs.

[05:22] Linda: Please note, we will require SOC2 artifacts and a data processing addendum for pilot. Also, we need clarity on log retention and whether any PII is stored.
[05:32] Maya: Understood. We'll send the SOC2 report, a standard DPA template, and a short note on log retention. By default Hosted keeps short-term logs for debugging; Dedicated/Private options allow longer retention under your control. We'll put that in the SOW.

[05:48] Rachel: How long does a pilot typically run and what ramp do you expect?
[05:52] Carlos: Typically 2-6 weeks. Short pilots (2-3 weeks) focus on quality/accuracy and basic latency checks. Longer pilots include integrations, canary routing and load tests. For Spectra, given the scope, I'd budget 4 weeks for the hosted validation and an additional 2-4 weeks if you choose Dedicated procurement and capacity setup.

[06:15] Samir: Procurement question — what lead times for Dedicated vs Private?
[06:19] Tom: Dedicated provisioning is usually 2-4 weeks after SOW/signature (depends on GPU availability and region). Private (VPC/on-prem) varies a lot — can be 6-12 weeks including security review and network validation. We'll surface these timelines in the SOW.

[06:35] Rachel: Cost sensitivity — is the $0.01/inference realistic? You mentioned quantization and batching — what's the typical delta?
[06:43] Tom: It depends on model size and QoS. With aggressive batching and 8-bit quantization on Dedicated, some customers see 2-3x cost reductions vs hosted. Hosted per-token rates are higher due to shared infra. We'll produce a cost model with assumptions: average input tokens 350, output 150, tokens per second, and show cost per 1M requests for each mode.

[07:06] Evan: For Dedicated, do we manage Kubernetes or do you provide managed runtime?
[07:10] Tom: We provide the inference runtime and manage GPU pools; you don't need to run your own K8s for our Dedicated offering. For Private on-prem we provide a package that integrates with your infra and can be deployed into your K8s or a managed appliance depending on the option.

[07:30] Linda: A few technical deep-dive asks: can you share p99 numbers for models at 350 tokens in your benchmarks, and what's your approach to KV cache management for chat-style workloads?
[07:40] Tom: We'll share example p99 numbers from similar customers. KV cache is handled by the runtime and supports checkpointing; it allows faster turnarounds for repeated conversations. For the fraud triage flow where prompt reuse is lower, caching benefits are modest, but for agent summaries where there's history it helps a lot.

[07:58] Rachel: Regarding model selection — do you manage model versions and rollouts? We want deterministic behavior in the pilot so we can attribute accuracy changes.
[08:06] Maya: Yes, version pinning and rollouts are supported. In Hosted you can pin a model version; Dedicated/Private gives you more control over which binary is deployed. We also support canarying and A/B rollouts with automatic fallback policies.

[08:20] Samir: For benchmarks, what metrics do you capture besides latency and accuracy?
[08:24] Tom: We'll capture throughput, GPU utilization, memory footprint, tokenized lengths distribution, and cost estimate. We'll also collect qualitative logs for error rates and failure modes.

[08:34] (brief crosstalk)

[08:40] Rachel: Ok so let's align on immediate artifacts we need from Redwood and what we will provide.

[08:45] Maya: From us: 1) SOC2 + security summary, 2) SOW & pilot pricing options, 3) benchmark plan and a checklist of sample data format, 4) example p99/p95 numbers from similar workloads. From Spectra: sample dataset (3-5k), traffic profile, security questionnaire answers.

[09:04] Linda: We'll also need your data deletion policy and confirmation that logs can be configured to exclude PII.

[09:10] Maya: We'll include that.

[09:14] Evan: One more edge-case — some of our transactions include small binary attachments; will that impact anything?
[09:20] Tom: Attachments per se are outside the LLM flow; you'd preprocess and send extracted text. We can help with recommended preprocess pipelines.

[09:30] Rachel: If we do Hosted pilot and it looks good, what's the typical migration path to Dedicated? Are there migration costs and downtime?
[09:36] Tom: Migration is usually straightforward — same API and model artifacts. For Dedicated you provision a reserved pool and we route traffic there; there can be some cutover coordination but no major downtime expected if planned. There may be one-time setup fees for Dedicated capacity depending on contract. We'll outline that in pricing.

[09:58] Samir: OK let's firm up timeline: we want initial hosted pilot within 2 weeks. Can Redwood start benchmark tests the week of Aug 17?

[10:05] Maya: Yes, assuming we get the dataset and traffic profile by Aug 14 we can schedule the lab benchmark for Aug 17-19. Tom will run tests and share results within 48 hours of the run.

[10:14] Tom: Quick note on benchmark scope: we'll run latency sweep at 1, 5, 15, 50, 120 qps, and a burst test up to 200 concurrent. We'll measure p50/p90/p95/p99 across those loads.

[10:26] Linda: We'll review the SOW for data residency clauses — Spectra requires EU data to remain in EU region. Does Redwood support region pinning?
[10:33] Maya: Yes, region pinning is supported across Hosted and Dedicated. Private gives full control of placement. We'll include region constraints in the SOW and pricing.

[10:42] Rachel: Any other risks we should call out now?
[10:44] Tom: GPU availability for Dedicated in specific regions can be a risk — we'll provide estimated timelines and alternatives. Also, model behavior drift — we'll suggest eval sets to catch regressions.

[10:55] Maya: Recap / next steps: Maya to send SOW/pricing and SOC2 pack by Aug 13; Tom to share benchmark plan by Aug 13 and then run lab tests week of Aug 17 assuming data arrives by Aug 14; Spectra to provide dataset and traffic profile by Aug 14; schedule 30-min benchmark review follow-up on Aug 20.

[11:18] Rachel: That works. Linda will review security docs and get back with outstanding questions.

[11:24] Samir: Thanks all. Sounds like a plan.

[11:28] Maya: Great, we'll follow up in email with calendar invites and links to the benchmark guide. Thanks everyone!

End of transcript.
